final_proof:
Proof. Let I=(-π,π], the half-open interval specified in the statement. For a nonzero vector a=(x,y), put r=√(x²+y²)>0. Its direction is the unique angle θ∈I satisfying (cos θ,sin θ)=(x/r,y/r). To see the asserted uniqueness, if θ,φ∈I have the same sine and cosine, then cos(θ−φ)=cos θ cos φ+sin θ sin φ=1. Hence θ−φ is an integral multiple of 2π. But θ−φ∈(-2π,2π), so θ=φ. It therefore suffices in every case to show that the displayed candidate belongs to I and has cosine x/r and sine y/r.

Recall that arctan is the inverse of tan restricted to (-π/2,π/2). Suppose first that x≠0, and set t=y/x and α=arctan(t). Then α∈(-π/2,π/2), tan α=t, and cos α>0. From 1+tan²α=1/cos²α, we obtain

cos α=1/√(1+t²),    sin α=t/√(1+t²).

If x>0, then √(1+t²)=r/x. Consequently cos α=x/r and sin α=y/r. Also α∈I, so uniqueness gives θ=α=arctan(y/x).

Now suppose x<0. Since |x|=-x, √(1+t²)=r/|x|, and the same formulas give

cos α=|x|/r=−x/r,    sin α=t|x|/r=−y/r.

Thus (x/r,y/r)=(−cos α,−sin α), and both α+π and α−π have the required cosine and sine. The representative in I is determined by the sign of y. If y≥0, then t=y/x≤0 and α∈(-π/2,0], so α+π∈(π/2,π]; hence θ=arctan(y/x)+π. This includes y=0, for which θ=π. If y<0, then t>0 and α∈(0,π/2), so α−π∈(-π,−π/2); hence θ=arctan(y/x)−π.

It remains to treat x=0. If y>0, then r=y and (x/r,y/r)=(0,1)=(cos(π/2),sin(π/2)), so θ=π/2. If y<0, then r=−y and (x/r,y/r)=(0,−1)=(cos(−π/2),sin(−π/2)), so θ=−π/2.

Finally, if x=y=0, the vector is zero. A direction would require the zero vector to be a positive scalar multiple of some unit vector (cos θ,sin θ), which is impossible after taking norms. Thus its direction is undefined. Combining the cases proves exactly the stated formula.
